newsitem.title: USA: Market war heats up as colds season arrives.
newsitem.headline: Market war heats up as colds season arrives.

text.p: If you are coughing and sneezing away these days, you are not alone. Believe it or not, at any given time there are about 39 million other Americans, or about 15 percent of the American public, who have colds, too.
This fact, though it might be a bit cruel to say, is good news for the makers of name-brand, cough-cold-allergy medications.

This is their big season and it will last into next April. But already, there are worries, with sales down due to price cuts, heavy competition and the ever-growing inroads of private-label or generic brands.

Accordingly, the producers of Tylenol, Robitusin, Benadryl, Sudafed, NyQuil and other well-known brands are now blasting away about the comparative advantages of their products over their competitors' on both television and in the print media.
Brands that hope to rise above the clutter are boosting ad budgets or finding other ways to get noticed.

A number of the big pharmaceuticals companies have jumped earlier into the season with hard-sell ads and given them an increased budget. For example, though it had relatively strong 1995-1996 sales, Bristol-Myers Squibb, which makes Comtrex, a multi-symptom medication, plans to boost its promotion of that product 50 percent during the rest of the 1996 season and through 1997.

While the companies jockey for positioning, the winner in this race could be determined, as in any horse race, by the weather. The cough-cold-allergy products traditionally rise or fall on the incidence of colds and flu.

In 1995, when the winter was pretty rough, sales rose 6 percent over 1994 when the winter temperatures and snowfall weren't as bad, according to Kline & Co., business consultants based in Fairfield, N.J.

"The market is growing but at a slower pace than in the past," said Laura Mahecha of the Kline office. "It's very much influenced by the prevalence of sickness. The producers can be expected to continue to advertise so that a particular brand will be top-of-the-mind when sickness occurs."

For the brand-name products, growth has disappeared. In the 52 weeks through Sept. 29, sales of the category totalled $1.8 billion in the nation's food, drug and mass merchandising stores, or 3.6 percent below the 1995 revenues, according to Information Resources, the market-research company in Chicago.

By contrast, private-label, store brand and generic medications are rising. Last year, their sales jumped 16 percent over the year before and industry sources think they are also doing better than brand-names of over-the-counter cold medications this year, too.

While the competition and market volatility can give marketers a headache, the prize is considerable: A market worth an estimated $2 billion, and still growing. In recent years, changes in the health care industry has Americans opting for self-medicating more than ever.
A rash of conversions from prescriptions to over-the-counter use has hastened the trend. About 60 percent of all medicines bought by consumers in the United States are non-prescription.

It will grow further, too, possibly sharply, if the Food and Drug Administration, which has oversight of such products, sets up a separate office to handle over-the-counter medication, a move that is being pushed by the industry.
Speeding the entry of drugs onto store shelves would give consumers more choices -- and add fodder to a marketing war already at its hottest level in history.
